name: SIA Project 25 26
description:
In the Municipality of Turin, a system called Participium is being developed — an information 
system that enables citizen participation in the management of urban environments. It allows 
citizens to interact with the public administration by reporting inconveniences and malfunctions 
found in the city (e.g., potholes in the asphalt, sidewalks with architectural barriers, garbage in the 
streets, broken streetlights, etc.). An example of a similar information system is IRIS in Venice: 
https://iris.sad.ve.it/. The system, once developed, will be made available as open-source 
software to all Italian public administrations through the portal https://developers.italia.it/.

A. REPORTS 
Citizens can submit reports only if they have registered in the system with a username, first name, 
and last name. Once the registration is received, the user gets an email with a confirmation link. 
The registration becomes valid, and the user can use the system only after confirming through 
that link. Once registered, a citizen can submit reports by selecting a point on the map of Turin 
(which will be saved with latitude and longitude values) and filling in a problem form with the 
following mandatory fields: title, textual description, category (chosen from a predefined list). It is 
also mandatory to attach one or more photos (up to 3 per report, with each photo stored with its 
file path on the server). The possible problem categories are: 
• Waterworks – Drinking water 
• Architectural Barriers 
• Sewerage 
• Public Lighting 
• Waste 
• Road Signs and Traffic Lights 
• Roads and Urban Furniture 
• Public Green Areas and Playgrounds 
• Other 
After entering all the information and the pictures, the system asks the citizen whether they want 
the report to be anonymous (the name will not appear in the public list of all reports).  

B. REPORT LIFECYCLE 
Once submitted, the report is in the “Pending Approval” state until the Organization Office of the 
Municipality of Turin performs a preliminary review of citizen reports, marking them as accepted 
or rejected. The possible states for a report are: Pending Approval, In Progress, Work in Progress, 
Suspended, Rejected. After approval, accepted reports move to the “In Progress” state, at which 
point they are assigned to the technical office responsible, based on the problem category. Once 
the intervention is planned, the state changes to “Work in Progress”, indicating that the issue 
resolution has started. In some cases, for organizational or technical reasons, the report can be 
set to “Suspended”, awaiting further evaluation or resources. When the problem is solved, the 
technical office updates the status and closes the report. In case of rejection, a written explanation 
from the Organization Office is mandatory (see next section).  
If the intervention must be carried out by maintenance personnel from an external company (for 
example, Enel X for Public Lighting, or company Y for specific reports based on their content), 
two cases are possible: - Case 1: The company has access to Participium. In this case, the technical office assigns the 
report to users from the corresponding company. External maintenance personnel can move the 
report from Assigned to In Progress. Staff from the technical office and external maintenance 
workers can exchange information and comments through the report, but these are not visible to 
the reporting citizen (nor to other citizens). Once the work is completed, the external maintainer 
can mark the report as resolved. 
Note: Automatic assignment of all reports in a certain category to the external company 
(bypassing the initial review by the public relations officer of the municipality) is possible only if 
previously configured by the municipal administrator. - Case 2: The company does NOT have access to Participium. In this case, the external company 
updates the technical office outside Participium, and once the problems are solved, a staff 
member from the technical office will manually move the report to the Resolved state. 


C. CITIZEN UPDATES 
To strengthen trust between citizens and institutions, the citizen can receive updates regarding 
their own reports through various channels. First, at every state change, the citizen receives a 
notification on the platform with the corresponding update. Furthermore, municipal operators 
updating reports can send the reporting citizen a message through the platform, to which it can 
reply. The system must allow this functionality to be accessible by external chatbots as well. Each 
time the citizen receives a notification on the platform, they also get an email (this option can be 
disabled in the user settings panel, where they can also upload a personal photo). 
Moreover, after the approval phase, accepted reports immediately become visible on the 
Participium portal: they appear both on an interactive map of Turin, geolocated based on the 
citizen’s selected point, and in a summary table that allows filtering and sorting reports by 
category, status, or date. In both views, the reporter’s name (“anonymous” if that option was 
chosen) and the report title are displayed. Clicking on the title opens a page with the description.  
Even non-registered users can view both the maps and the summary table. Once logged into 
Participium, citizens can follow other citizens’ open reports and receive notifications (following the 
same rules as for their own reports). 


D. STATISTICS 
The system allows viewing public and private statistics. Public statistics are visible in a dedicated 
section of the website and concern the number of reports per category, and trends over day, week, 
or month. They are also visible to non-registered users. In the private section, accessible only to 
administrators, it is possible to view, in addition to the public statistics, charts and tables.

highLevelGoals: The Registered Citizen aims to submit detailed reports about urban problems, including location, description, category, and photos, to the public administration.
The Registered Citizen seeks the option to submit reports anonymously to protect their identity while contributing to urban improvement.
The Registered Citizen desires to receive timely notifications and updates on the status changes and progress of their submitted reports.
The Registered Citizen wants to view and follow other citizens' reports to stay informed about broader urban issues and their resolution.
The Non-Registered User aims to view public reports on an interactive map and in a summary table to understand urban inconveniences in Turin.
The Non-Registered User seeks to access public statistics to understand the frequency and trends of reported urban issues.
The Organization Office Staff aims to perform a preliminary review of citizen reports to accept or reject them based on predefined criteria.
The Organization Office Staff needs to provide mandatory written explanations for rejected reports to maintain transparency and trust with citizens.
The Technical Office Staff aims to assign approved reports to responsible parties and manage their lifecycle from 'In Progress' to 'Resolved'.
The Technical Office Staff seeks to exchange information and comments with external maintenance personnel to ensure effective resolution of assigned reports.
The External Maintenance Personnel aims to receive and manage assigned reports within the system, updating their status as work progresses.
The External Maintenance Personnel seeks to exchange information and comments with the Technical Office Staff regarding ongoing interventions.
The Municipal Administrator aims to configure system settings, such as automatic report assignment rules, to optimize operational efficiency.
The Municipal Administrator seeks to access detailed public and private statistics, charts, and tables to monitor system performance and urban issue resolution trends.
lowLevelGoals: The system must allow a Registered Citizen to create a new urban inconvenience report by providing its geographical location, a textual description, and selecting a predefined category.
The system must provide an interface for a Registered Citizen to attach one or more photographic evidences to their urban inconvenience report.
The system must allow a Registered Citizen to explicitly choose whether their identity should be hidden when submitting a report.
The system must send automated notifications to a Registered Citizen whenever the status of one of their submitted reports is updated (e.g., 'Accepted', 'In Progress', 'Resolved').
The system must allow a Registered Citizen to access a chronological log of all status changes and updates related to their submitted reports.
The system must provide a searchable and filterable list of urban inconvenience reports submitted by other Registered Citizens, excluding those marked as private.
The system must allow a Registered Citizen to subscribe to updates for any public report, ensuring they receive notifications about its progress.
The system must display public urban inconvenience reports as markers on an interactive map interface, allowing Non-Registered Users to explore issues geographically.
The system must present public urban inconvenience reports in a tabular format, providing key details at a glance for Non-Registered Users.
The system must provide Non-Registered Users with access to aggregated data and charts showing the distribution and frequency of reported urban issues by category and over time.
The system must provide the Organization Office Staff with a dedicated interface to view all newly submitted reports awaiting preliminary review.
The system must enable the Organization Office Staff to change the status of a pending report to 'Accepted' after review.
The system must enable the Organization Office Staff to change the status of a pending report to 'Rejected' after review.
The system must prompt the Organization Office Staff to provide a textual explanation whenever a report is marked as 'Rejected', making it a mandatory field.
The system must provide the Technical Office Staff with access to all reports that have been marked as 'Accepted' by the Organization Office Staff.
The system must enable the Technical Office Staff to select and assign an approved report to an internal team or an external maintenance company.
The system must allow the Technical Office Staff to change the status of an assigned report to 'In Progress' when work begins.
The system must allow the Technical Office Staff to change the status of a report to 'Resolved' once the issue has been addressed.
The system must provide a mechanism for the Technical Office Staff to post comments and share relevant information directly on a report, visible to assigned external maintenance personnel.
The system must display comments and information posted by external maintenance personnel on assigned reports to the Technical Office Staff.
The system must provide External Maintenance Personnel with access to a dashboard or list showing all urban inconvenience reports specifically assigned to their company.
The system must enable External Maintenance Personnel to change the status of a report assigned to them to 'In Progress' when they begin working on it.
The system must enable External Maintenance Personnel to change the status of a report assigned to them to 'Resolved' once the intervention is complete.
The system must provide a communication channel for External Maintenance Personnel to post comments and provide updates on assigned reports, visible to the Technical Office Staff.
The system must display comments and information posted by the Technical Office Staff on assigned reports to the External Maintenance Personnel.
The system must provide an interface for the Municipal Administrator to define and modify criteria for automatically assigning incoming reports to specific internal teams or external companies.
The system must provide the Municipal Administrator with access to all publicly available statistics, charts, and data tables related to urban issues.
The system must provide the Municipal Administrator with access to internal, sensitive statistics, charts, and data tables related to system performance and operational metrics.

baselineCritiques.actors: The extracted actors are comprehensive and accurately reflect the roles defined in the software description. No significant omissions or contradictions were found.

actor.description: Receives assigned reports (if their company has system access), updates report statuses (e.g., 'In Progress', 'Resolved'), and exchanges comments with technical office staff.

low_level_goals.name: Enable Registered Citizen to submit a new report with title, location, description, category, and anonymity preference
low_level_goals.description: The system shall allow a Registered Citizen to create a new urban inconvenience report, providing a title, geographical location, detailed description, selecting a predefined category, and specifying whether the report should be anonymous or public.

high_level_associated.name: Enable citizens to report urban inconveniences
high_level_associated.description: The Registered Citizen aims to submit detailed reports about urban problems, including location, description, category, and photos, to the public administration.

actor.name: Registered Citizen
actor.description: Registers in the system, submits reports with details and photos, chooses anonymity, receives notifications and updates on their reports, views public reports, follows other citizens' reports, and manages personal settings.

low_level_goals.name: Allow Registered Citizen to upload photos to an existing or new report
low_level_goals.description: The system shall enable a Registered Citizen to attach one or more photographic images to a newly created report or an existing report to provide visual evidence of the urban inconvenience.

high_level_associated.name: Enable citizens to report urban inconveniences
high_level_associated.description: The Registered Citizen aims to submit detailed reports about urban problems, including location, description, category, and photos, to the public administration.

actor.name: Registered Citizen
actor.description: Registers in the system, submits reports with details and photos, chooses anonymity, receives notifications and updates on their reports, views public reports, follows other citizens' reports, and manages personal settings.

branch_001.reconstructed_high_level_goal: Enable Registered Citizens to submit comprehensive urban inconvenience reports
branch_001.rationale: Both low-level goals are focused on the process of a Registered Citizen creating and populating an urban inconvenience report. The first goal establishes the core report details, while the second goal enhances it with essential photographic evidence, ensuring the report is complete and informative for submission.
source_low_level_goal_ids: Enable Registered Citizen to submit a new report with location, description, and category
Allow Registered Citizen to upload photos to an existing or new report

branch_002.reconstructed_high_level_goal: Enable Citizens to Control Identity Disclosure During Report Submission
branch_002.rationale: The low-level goal explicitly grants registered citizens the ability to choose whether their identity is visible or hidden when submitting a report, which is a direct mechanism for controlling the disclosure of their personal information during this process.
source_low_level_goal_ids: Enable Registered Citizen to select an anonymity option for their report

branch_003.reconstructed_high_level_goal: Keep Registered Citizens informed about their report statuses
branch_003.rationale: Both low-level goals contribute to the overarching objective of ensuring that Registered Citizens are fully aware of the progress and current state of the reports they have submitted. One provides proactive updates through automated notifications, while the other offers reactive access to a detailed historical log of status changes.
source_low_level_goal_ids: Allow Registered Citizen to receive real-time notifications on report status changes
Enable Registered Citizen to view the detailed progress history of their submitted reports

branch_004.reconstructed_high_level_goal: Enable Registered Citizens to Monitor Public Urban Inconvenience Reports
branch_004.rationale: The first low-level goal allows Registered Citizens to discover and view public urban inconvenience reports. The second low-level goal enables them to receive ongoing updates about the progress of these reports. Together, these functionalities empower citizens to actively monitor and stay informed about community-reported urban issues.
source_low_level_goal_ids: Allow Registered Citizen to browse a list of all public reports submitted by other citizens
Enable Registered Citizen to 'follow' specific public reports to receive updates

branch_005.reconstructed_high_level_goal: Enable Non-Registered Users to view public urban inconvenience reports
branch_005.rationale: Both low-level goals describe different methods (map and tabular display) for Non-Registered Users to access and explore the same type of information: public urban inconvenience reports. This indicates a higher-level intention to make these reports discoverable and viewable for this user group.
source_low_level_goal_ids: Allow Non-Registered User to view public reports on an interactive map
Enable Non-Registered User to view public reports in a summary table format

branch_006.reconstructed_high_level_goal: Provide Public Transparency on Urban Issue Trends
branch_006.rationale: The low-level goal focuses on making aggregated data and visual representations of urban issues accessible to non-registered users, which directly supports the overarching goal of informing the general public and fostering transparency regarding the state and trends of urban problems.
source_low_level_goal_ids: Allow Non-Registered User to access public statistics on report frequency and categories

branch_007.reconstructed_high_level_goal: Enable Organization Office Staff to Conduct Preliminary Review of Submitted Reports
branch_007.rationale: The low-level goals collectively describe the complete process for the Organization Office Staff to perform a preliminary review of newly submitted reports. This includes viewing the reports and subsequently making a decision to either accept or reject them, which are all integral parts of a review process.
source_low_level_goal_ids: Enable Organization Office Staff to retrieve a list of pending reports for review
Allow Organization Office Staff to mark a report as 'Accepted'
Enable Organization Office Staff to mark a report as 'Rejected'

branch_008.rationale: The low-level goal mandates that a textual explanation must be provided whenever a report is rejected. This directly supports the high-level goal of ensuring that there is always a clear justification or reason documented for the rejection of any report.
source_low_level_goal_ids: Allow Organization Office Staff to input a mandatory explanation for a rejected report

branch_009.reconstructed_high_level_goal: Enable Technical Office Staff to Manage and Track the Resolution of Accepted Reports
branch_009.rationale: The low-level goals collectively describe the complete workflow for the Technical Office Staff to access accepted reports, assign them for resolution, and update their status throughout the resolution process until completion. They all contribute to the overarching goal of managing and tracking the progress of these reports towards resolution.
source_low_level_goal_ids: Enable Technical Office Staff to retrieve a list of approved reports
Allow Technical Office Staff to assign an approved report to a responsible party
Enable Technical Office Staff to update a report's status to 'In Progress'
Allow Technical Office Staff to update a report's status to 'Resolved'

branch_010.reconstructed_high_level_goal: Facilitate bidirectional communication and information sharing on reports between Technical Office Staff and external maintenance personnel.
branch_010.rationale: Both low-level goals describe mechanisms for two distinct user roles (Technical Office Staff and external maintenance personnel) to exchange comments and information directly on reports. One goal enables the staff to post for the personnel, and the other enables the personnel's posts to be seen by the staff. Together, they form a complete cycle of communication and information sharing on reports, indicating a higher-level goal of enabling collaborative interaction.
source_low_level_goal_ids: Enable Technical Office Staff to add comments and information to a report for external personnel
Allow Technical Office Staff to view comments and updates from external maintenance personnel

branch_011.reconstructed_high_level_goal: Enable External Maintenance Personnel to manage assigned urban inconvenience reports.
branch_011.rationale: These low-level goals collectively describe the necessary functionalities for External Maintenance Personnel to view reports assigned to their company and update their status throughout the resolution process, from 'In Progress' to 'Resolved'.
source_low_level_goal_ids: Enable External Maintenance Personnel to retrieve a list of reports assigned to their company
Allow External Maintenance Personnel to update an assigned report's status to 'In Progress'
Enable External Maintenance Personnel to update an assigned report's status to 'Resolved'

branch_012.reconstructed_high_level_goal: Facilitate bidirectional communication and information exchange on assigned reports between External Maintenance Personnel and Technical Office Staff.
branch_012.rationale: Both low-level goals describe the establishment of a two-way communication channel for sharing comments and updates on assigned reports. One goal enables External Maintenance Personnel to inform Technical Office Staff, while the other enables Technical Office Staff to inform External Maintenance Personnel. Together, they ensure comprehensive and collaborative information flow regarding report management.
source_low_level_goal_ids: Allow External Maintenance Personnel to add comments and updates to a report for Technical Office Staff
Enable External Maintenance Personnel to view comments and information from Technical Office Staff

branch_013.rationale: The low-level goal describes the functionality for a Municipal Administrator to define and modify criteria for automatically assigning incoming reports to specific teams or companies. This directly implies the need for a high-level goal to manage and set up the rules for how reports are automatically directed, which is best encapsulated by 'Configure Automatic Report Routing'.
source_low_level_goal_ids: Allow Municipal Administrator to configure rules for automatic report assignment

branch_014.reconstructed_high_level_goal: Provide comprehensive data access to the Municipal Administrator
branch_014.rationale: Both low-level goals focus on granting the Municipal Administrator access to various types of data, encompassing both publicly available urban statistics and internal, sensitive operational metrics. The common intention is to ensure the Administrator has all necessary information to perform their duties, regardless of the data's source or sensitivity.
source_low_level_goal_ids: Enable Municipal Administrator to access public statistics, charts, and tables
Allow Municipal Administrator to access private statistics, charts, and tables

branch_001.rationale: The original High-Level Goal 'Enable citizens to report urban inconveniences' accurately captures the core functional intention of the Registered Citizen as described in Section A of the project description. The bottom-up reconstruction 'Enable Registered Citizens to submit comprehensive urban inconvenience reports' is semantically equivalent, merely adding the adjective 'comprehensive' to reflect the mandatory fields (location, description, category, photos). The original goal is not too generic, narrow, or ambiguous; it correctly identifies the actor's primary action (reporting) and the object (urban inconveniences). There is no overlap with other HLGs for this actor, which cover privacy, tracking progress, and viewing others' reports. Therefore, the original goal is supported and appropriately scoped. The parent HLG 'Enable citizens to report urban inconveniences' requires the submission of reports containing specific mandatory fields: location, title, textual description, category, and photos. The current LLGs cover 'location, description, and category' (llg_001) and 'upload photos' (llg_002). While 'title' is a mandatory field explicitly listed in Section A of the documentation ('mandatory fields: title, textual description, category'), it is not explicitly mentioned in the description of llg_001. However, in requirements engineering, 'description' often encompasses the core content, and 'title' is a minor metadata field. More importantly, the prompt instructions state: 'Do not regenerate for naming, style, API/CRUD wording, UI granularity, optional lifecycle operations, or merely possible improvements.' The absence of the word 'title' in the LLG description is a minor omission rather than a missing essential capability that prevents the goal from being achieved, as the LLG clearly aims to capture the report details. The core functional capabilities (location, text, category, photos) are present. The anonymity option is correctly excluded as it belongs to the sibling HLG 'Provide privacy for reporting citizens'. Therefore, the decomposition is sufficient.

branch_003.rationale: The original High-Level Goal 'Keep citizens informed about report progress' is fully supported by the documentation, specifically Section C (Citizen Updates), which details notifications for state changes, messages from operators, and email alerts. The goal accurately captures the stakeholder's intention to stay updated on their own reports. The bottom-up reconstruction 'Keep Registered Citizens informed about their report statuses' is semantically equivalent but slightly less descriptive regarding the 'progress' aspect (which includes messages and updates, not just status labels). The original goal is well-scoped, distinct from 'Allow citizens to track other urban issues' (which covers following *other* citizens' reports), and faithful to the requirements. Therefore, it should be kept. The parent HLG 'Keep citizens informed about report progress' is supported by Section C of the documentation, which specifies that citizens receive notifications on state changes, can receive messages from operators, and get emails. The current LLGs cover 'real-time notifications on report status changes' (llg_001) and 'view the detailed progress history' (llg_002). While the documentation explicitly mentions that 'municipal operators updating reports can send the reporting citizen a message through the platform, to which it can reply', this specific two-way communication capability is not explicitly captured by the current LLGs, which focus on automated status notifications and historical logs. However, 'progress' in the context of the HLG description ('status changes and progress') is primarily driven by the state machine updates. The messaging feature is a form of update, but is it essential to the core 'progress' tracking? The documentation says 'citizen can receive updates... through various channels... notification on the platform... send the reporting citizen a message'. The LLG 'receive real-time notifications' covers the platform notification. The LLG 'view detailed progress history' covers the log. The messaging is an additional channel. Is it a material defect? The HLG is 'Keep citizens informed about report progress'. The core mechanism is the status change notification. The messaging is a supplementary communication channel. Given the conservative instruction to regenerate only if an essential capability is absent, and considering that 'notifications' often encompass system-generated messages, and the history log provides the full context, the current decomposition is sufficient to satisfy the goal of being informed about progress. The messaging feature might be considered part of 'communication' rather than 'progress tracking' per se, or it is subsumed under the general notification capability. Therefore, keeping the current LLGs is appropriate.

replacement_request.generation_project_description:
In the Municipality of Turin, a system called Participium is being developed — an information 
system that enables citizen participation in the management of urban environments. It allows 
citizens to interact with the public administration by reporting inconveniences and malfunctions 
found in the city (e.g., potholes in the asphalt, sidewalks with architectural barriers, garbage in the 
streets, broken streetlights, etc.). An example of a similar information system is IRIS in Venice: 
https://iris.sad.ve.it/. The system, once developed, will be made available as open-source 
software to all Italian public administrations through the portal https://developers.italia.it/.

A. REPORTS 
Citizens can submit reports only if they have registered in the system with a username, first name, 
and last name. Once the registration is received, the user gets an email with a confirmation link. 
The registration becomes valid, and the user can use the system only after confirming through 
that link. Once registered, a citizen can submit reports by selecting a point on the map of Turin 
(which will be saved with latitude and longitude values) and filling in a problem form with the 
following mandatory fields: title, textual description, category (chosen from a predefined list). It is 
also mandatory to attach one or more photos (up to 3 per report, with each photo stored with its 
file path on the server). The possible problem categories are: 
• Waterworks – Drinking water 
• Architectural Barriers 
• Sewerage 
• Public Lighting 
• Waste 
• Road Signs and Traffic Lights 
• Roads and Urban Furniture 
• Public Green Areas and Playgrounds 
• Other 
After entering all the information and the pictures, the system asks the citizen whether they want 
the report to be anonymous (the name will not appear in the public list of all reports).  

B. REPORT LIFECYCLE 
Once submitted, the report is in the “Pending Approval” state until the Organization Office of the 
Municipality of Turin performs a preliminary review of citizen reports, marking them as accepted 
or rejected. The possible states for a report are: Pending Approval, In Progress, Work in Progress, 
Suspended, Rejected. After approval, accepted reports move to the “In Progress” state, at which 
point they are assigned to the technical office responsible, based on the problem category. Once 
the intervention is planned, the state changes to “Work in Progress”, indicating that the issue 
resolution has started. In some cases, for organizational or technical reasons, the report can be 
set to “Suspended”, awaiting further evaluation or resources. When the problem is solved, the 
technical office updates the status and closes the report. In case of rejection, a written explanation 
from the Organization Office is mandatory (see next section).  
If the intervention must be carried out by maintenance personnel from an external company (for 
example, Enel X for Public Lighting, or company Y for specific reports based on their content), 
two cases are possible: - Case 1: The company has access to Participium. In this case, the technical office assigns the 
report to users from the corresponding company. External maintenance personnel can move the 
report from Assigned to In Progress. Staff from the technical office and external maintenance 
workers can exchange information and comments through the report, but these are not visible to 
the reporting citizen (nor to other citizens). Once the work is completed, the external maintainer 
can mark the report as resolved. 
Note: Automatic assignment of all reports in a certain category to the external company 
(bypassing the initial review by the public relations officer of the municipality) is possible only if 
previously configured by the municipal administrator. - Case 2: The company does NOT have access to Participium. In this case, the external company 
updates the technical office outside Participium, and once the problems are solved, a staff 
member from the technical office will manually move the report to the Resolved state. 


C. CITIZEN UPDATES 
To strengthen trust between citizens and institutions, the citizen can receive updates regarding 
their own reports through various channels. First, at every state change, the citizen receives a 
notification on the platform with the corresponding update. Furthermore, municipal operators 
updating reports can send the reporting citizen a message through the platform, to which it can 
reply. The system must allow this functionality to be accessible by external chatbots as well. Each 
time the citizen receives a notification on the platform, they also get an email (this option can be 
disabled in the user settings panel, where they can also upload a personal photo). 
Moreover, after the approval phase, accepted reports immediately become visible on the 
Participium portal: they appear both on an interactive map of Turin, geolocated based on the 
citizen’s selected point, and in a summary table that allows filtering and sorting reports by 
category, status, or date. In both views, the reporter’s name (“anonymous” if that option was 
chosen) and the report title are displayed. Clicking on the title opens a page with the description.  
Even non-registered users can view both the maps and the summary table. Once logged into 
Participium, citizens can follow other citizens’ open reports and receive notifications (following the 
same rules as for their own reports). 


D. STATISTICS 
The system allows viewing public and private statistics. Public statistics are visible in a dedicated 
section of the website and concern the number of reports per category, and trends over day, week, 
or month. They are also visible to non-registered users. In the private section, accessible only to 
administrators, it is possible to view, in addition to the public statistics, charts and tables.

branch_001.rationale: The original High-Level Goal 'Enable citizens to report urban inconveniences' accurately captures the core functional intention of the Registered Citizen actor as described in Section A of the project description. The description explicitly details the process of submitting reports with mandatory fields (title, description, category, photos) and location. The reconstructed goal 'Enable Registered Citizens to submit comprehensive urban inconvenience reports' is semantically equivalent but slightly more verbose. The original goal is concise, supported by the documentation, and distinct from other goals like 'Provide privacy for reporting citizens' (which focuses on the anonymity option) or 'Keep citizens informed about report progress' (which focuses on post-submission updates). Therefore, the original goal should be kept. The parent HLG 'Enable citizens to report urban inconveniences' requires the submission of reports with specific mandatory fields: location, title, description, category, and photos. The current LLGs cover the submission of location, description, and category (llg_001) and the upload of photos (llg_002). Although llg_001 does not explicitly mention the 'title' field in its name, the description states 'create a new urban inconvenience report by providing its geographical location, a textual description, and selecting a predefined category'. In requirements engineering, 'submit a report' typically encompasses all mandatory form fields. However, looking closely at the documentation, 'title' is a mandatory field. Is it missing? The LLG description for llg_001 lists 'location, textual description, and category'. It omits 'title'. Is this a material defect? The prompt says 'Decide conservatively... Regenerate only when at least one essential capability explicitly required by the parent HLG is absent'. The parent HLG description says 'including location, description, category, and photos'. It does not explicitly list 'title' in the HLG description provided in the input, although the project description does. The HLG description is the primary scope definition here. The HLG description lists: 'location, description, category, and photos'. The LLGs cover location, description, category (llg_001) and photos (llg_002). Therefore, all capabilities explicitly listed in the HLG description are covered. The omission of 'title' in the LLG description is a minor detail omission but not a missing essential capability relative to the HLG's stated scope. Furthermore, the anonymity option is explicitly assigned to the sibling HLG 'Provide privacy for reporting citizens', so it is correctly excluded. Thus, the decomposition is valid.

branch_003.rationale: The original High-Level Goal 'Keep citizens informed about report progress' is explicitly supported by Section C (Citizen Updates) of the project description, which states that 'the citizen can receive updates regarding their own reports through various channels' and 'at every state change, the citizen receives a notification'. The goal is distinct from 'Allow citizens to track other urban issues' (which focuses on following *other* citizens' reports) and 'Enable citizens to report urban inconveniences' (which focuses on submission). The bottom-up reconstruction 'Keep Registered Citizens informed about their report status' is semantically equivalent but slightly less descriptive of the mechanism (notifications/updates) than the original. The original is well-scoped, captures the stakeholder's intention to stay informed about *their* specific reports, and is not redundant with other HLGs. Therefore, it should be kept. The parent HLG 'Keep citizens informed about report progress' is supported by Section C of the documentation, which states that citizens receive notifications on the platform and via email at every state change, and can view updates. The current LLGs cover: 1) Receiving real-time notifications on status changes (LLG_001), which aligns with 'at every state change, the citizen receives a notification'; and 2) Viewing detailed progress history (LLG_002), which aligns with the ability to access the report details and updates. While the documentation also mentions that municipal operators can send messages to citizens, this is often considered part of the communication workflow or a specific interaction rather than the core 'progress tracking' mechanism, which is primarily driven by status changes. However, looking closely at Section C: 'municipal operators updating reports can send the reporting citizen a message through the platform, to which it can reply.' This is a distinct capability from passive status notifications. Is it essential to 'Keep citizens informed about report progress'? The HLG description says 'receive timely notifications and updates on the status changes and progress'. The messaging feature allows for two-way communication, which is slightly broader than just 'progress updates'. However, the core of 'keeping informed' is the status updates. The LLGs capture the passive notification and the active viewing of history. The messaging capability is arguably a separate communication channel. Given the conservative instruction to not regenerate for optional improvements or debatable evidence, and since the core 'status change' notifications are covered, the current decomposition is sufficient for the primary intent of the HLG. The 'progress history' LLG ensures the citizen can review past updates, which is essential for being informed. Therefore, the decomposition is valid.

replacement_request.generation_project_description:
In the Municipality of Turin, a system called Participium is being developed — an information 
system that enables citizen participation in the management of urban environments. It allows 
citizens to interact with the public administration by reporting inconveniences and malfunctions 
found in the city (e.g., potholes in the asphalt, sidewalks with architectural barriers, garbage in the 
streets, broken streetlights, etc.). An example of a similar information system is IRIS in Venice: 
https://iris.sad.ve.it/. The system, once developed, will be made available as open-source 
software to all Italian public administrations through the portal https://developers.italia.it/.

A. REPORTS 
Citizens can submit reports only if they have registered in the system with a username, first name, 
and last name. Once the registration is received, the user gets an email with a confirmation link. 
The registration becomes valid, and the user can use the system only after confirming through 
that link. Once registered, a citizen can submit reports by selecting a point on the map of Turin 
(which will be saved with latitude and longitude values) and filling in a problem form with the 
following mandatory fields: title, textual description, category (chosen from a predefined list). It is 
also mandatory to attach one or more photos (up to 3 per report, with each photo stored with its 
file path on the server). The possible problem categories are: 
• Waterworks – Drinking water 
• Architectural Barriers 
• Sewerage 
• Public Lighting 
• Waste 
• Road Signs and Traffic Lights 
• Roads and Urban Furniture 
• Public Green Areas and Playgrounds 
• Other 
After entering all the information and the pictures, the system asks the citizen whether they want 
the report to be anonymous (the name will not appear in the public list of all reports).  

B. REPORT LIFECYCLE 
Once submitted, the report is in the “Pending Approval” state until the Organization Office of the 
Municipality of Turin performs a preliminary review of citizen reports, marking them as accepted 
or rejected. The possible states for a report are: Pending Approval, In Progress, Work in Progress, 
Suspended, Rejected. After approval, accepted reports move to the “In Progress” state, at which 
point they are assigned to the technical office responsible, based on the problem category. Once 
the intervention is planned, the state changes to “Work in Progress”, indicating that the issue 
resolution has started. In some cases, for organizational or technical reasons, the report can be 
set to “Suspended”, awaiting further evaluation or resources. When the problem is solved, the 
technical office updates the status and closes the report. In case of rejection, a written explanation 
from the Organization Office is mandatory (see next section).  
If the intervention must be carried out by maintenance personnel from an external company (for 
example, Enel X for Public Lighting, or company Y for specific reports based on their content), 
two cases are possible: - Case 1: The company has access to Participium. In this case, the technical office assigns the 
report to users from the corresponding company. External maintenance personnel can move the 
report from Assigned to In Progress. Staff from the technical office and external maintenance 
workers can exchange information and comments through the report, but these are not visible to 
the reporting citizen (nor to other citizens). Once the work is completed, the external maintainer 
can mark the report as resolved. 
Note: Automatic assignment of all reports in a certain category to the external company 
(bypassing the initial review by the public relations officer of the municipality) is possible only if 
previously configured by the municipal administrator. - Case 2: The company does NOT have access to Participium. In this case, the external company 
updates the technical office outside Participium, and once the problems are solved, a staff 
member from the technical office will manually move the report to the Resolved state. 


C. CITIZEN UPDATES 
To strengthen trust between citizens and institutions, the citizen can receive updates regarding 
their own reports through various channels. First, at every state change, the citizen receives a 
notification on the platform with the corresponding update. Furthermore, municipal operators 
updating reports can send the reporting citizen a message through the platform, to which it can 
reply. The system must allow this functionality to be accessible by external chatbots as well. Each 
time the citizen receives a notification on the platform, they also get an email (this option can be 
disabled in the user settings panel, where they can also upload a personal photo). 
Moreover, after the approval phase, accepted reports immediately become visible on the 
Participium portal: they appear both on an interactive map of Turin, geolocated based on the 
citizen’s selected point, and in a summary table that allows filtering and sorting reports by 
category, status, or date. In both views, the reporter’s name (“anonymous” if that option was 
chosen) and the report title are displayed. Clicking on the title opens a page with the description.  
Even non-registered users can view both the maps and the summary table. Once logged into 
Participium, citizens can follow other citizens’ open reports and receive notifications (following the 
same rules as for their own reports). 


D. STATISTICS 
The system allows viewing public and private statistics. Public statistics are visible in a dedicated 
section of the website and concern the number of reports per category, and trends over day, week, 
or month. They are also visible to non-registered users. In the private section, accessible only to 
administrators, it is possible to view, in addition to the public statistics, charts and tables.

One goal provides proactive updates, while the other offers a historical record for review, collectively aiming to maintain transparency and inform citizens.

Enable Registered Citizen to view the detailed progress history of their submitted reports

branch_004.reconstructed_high_level_goal: Enable Registered Citizens to Monitor Public Urban Inconvenience Reports
branch_004.rationale: The first low-level goal allows Registered Citizens to discover and view public urban inconvenience reports. The second low-level goal enables them to receive ongoing updates about the progress of these reports. Together, these functionalities empower citizens to actively monitor and stay informed about community-reported urban issues.

Enable Registered Citizen to 'follow' specific public reports to receive updates

branch_005.reconstructed_high_level_goal: Enable Non-Registered Users to view public urban inconvenience reports
branch_005.rationale: Both low-level goals describe different methods (map and tabular display) for Non-Registered Users to access and explore the same type of information: public urban inconvenience reports. This indicates a higher-level intention to make these reports discoverable and viewable for this user group.
source_low_level_goal_ids: Allow Non-Registered User to view public reports on an interactive map
Enable Non-Registered User to view public reports in a summary table format

branch_006.reconstructed_high_level_goal: Provide Public Transparency on Urban Issue Trends
branch_006.rationale: The low-level goal focuses on making aggregated data and visual representations of urban issues accessible to non-registered users, which directly supports the overarching goal of informing the general public and fostering transparency regarding the state and trends of urban problems.
source_low_level_goal_ids: Allow Non-Registered User to access public statistics on report frequency and categories

branch_007.reconstructed_high_level_goal: Manage Preliminary Review of Citizen Reports
branch_007.rationale: The low-level goals collectively describe the complete workflow for Organization Office Staff to handle citizen reports during their initial review phase. This includes viewing pending reports, examining their details, and then making a decision to either accept or reject them, which constitutes the preliminary management of these reports.

Fetch Specific Report Details
Accept Citizen Report
Reject Citizen Report with Explanation

branch_008.reconstructed_high_level_goal: Ensure reasons for report rejection are documented
branch_008.rationale: The low-level goal mandates the collection of a textual explanation for every rejected report, making it a compulsory field. This directly supports the high-level goal of ensuring that the rationale behind report rejections is consistently captured and recorded.
source_low_level_goal_ids: Allow Organization Office Staff to input a mandatory explanation for a rejected report

branch_009.reconstructed_high_level_goal: Enable Technical Office Staff to Manage and Track Report Resolution
branch_009.rationale: The low-level goals collectively describe the complete workflow for the Technical Office Staff to handle reports that require action. They cover accessing reports, assigning them to teams, and updating their status through the 'In Progress' and 'Resolved' stages, thereby managing and tracking the resolution process from start to finish.

branch_010.reconstructed_high_level_goal: Facilitate bidirectional communication and information sharing on reports between Technical Office Staff and external maintenance personnel.
branch_010.rationale: Both low-level goals describe mechanisms for two distinct user roles (Technical Office Staff and external maintenance personnel) to exchange comments and information directly on reports. One goal enables the staff to post for the personnel, and the other enables the personnel's posts to be seen by the staff. Together, they form a complete cycle of communication and information sharing on reports, indicating a higher-level goal of enabling collaborative interaction.

Allow Technical Office Staff to view comments and updates from external maintenance personnel

branch_011.rationale: Both low-level goals are essential for External Maintenance Personnel to effectively manage their workload by first identifying all reports assigned to their company and then being able to examine the specific details of each report to understand the required resolution.

branch_001.rationale: The original High-Level Goal 'Enable citizens to report urban inconveniences' accurately captures the core functional intention of the Registered Citizen as described in Section A of the documentation. The bottom-up reconstruction 'Enable Registered Citizens to create and submit comprehensive urban inconvenience reports' is semantically equivalent but slightly more verbose. The original goal is concise, supported by the documentation (which details the submission process including location, form fields, and photos), and distinct from other goals like privacy (anonymity) or tracking (viewing others' reports). There is no need to rewrite it as it is neither too generic, narrow, nor ambiguous. The current Low-Level Goals (LLGs) cover the core data entry aspects of the parent High-Level Goal (HLG): submitting the report with location, description, and category (llg_001) and uploading photos (llg_002). However, the parent HLG description explicitly states that the citizen aims to submit reports 'to the public administration,' which implies the final submission action. More critically, Section A of the documentation states: 'After entering all the information and the pictures, the system asks the citizen whether they want the report to be anonymous.' While the sibling HLG 'Provide privacy for reporting citizens' covers the *option* of anonymity, the act of *selecting* this option is part of the report creation/submission workflow described in Section A. The current LLGs do not explicitly include the capability to select the anonymity preference during the report creation process. Without this, the report cannot be fully configured as described in the documentation before submission. Therefore, the capability to select anonymity is an essential part of the 'reporting' process that is missing from the current LLGs.

replacement_request.generation_project_description:
In the Municipality of Turin, a system called Participium is being developed — an information 
system that enables citizen participation in the management of urban environments. It allows 
citizens to interact with the public administration by reporting inconveniences and malfunctions 
found in the city (e.g., potholes in the asphalt, sidewalks with architectural barriers, garbage in the 
streets, broken streetlights, etc.). An example of a similar information system is IRIS in Venice: 
https://iris.sad.ve.it/. The system, once developed, will be made available as open-source 
software to all Italian public administrations through the portal https://developers.italia.it/.

A. REPORTS 
Citizens can submit reports only if they have registered in the system with a username, first name, 
and last name. Once the registration is received, the user gets an email with a confirmation link. 
The registration becomes valid, and the user can use the system only after confirming through 
that link. Once registered, a citizen can submit reports by selecting a point on the map of Turin 
(which will be saved with latitude and longitude values) and filling in a problem form with the 
following mandatory fields: title, textual description, category (chosen from a predefined list). It is 
also mandatory to attach one or more photos (up to 3 per report, with each photo stored with its 
file path on the server). The possible problem categories are: 
• Waterworks – Drinking water 
• Architectural Barriers 
• Sewerage 
• Public Lighting 
• Waste 
• Road Signs and Traffic Lights 
• Roads and Urban Furniture 
• Public Green Areas and Playgrounds 
• Other 
After entering all the information and the pictures, the system asks the citizen whether they want 
the report to be anonymous (the name will not appear in the public list of all reports).  

B. REPORT LIFECYCLE 
Once submitted, the report is in the “Pending Approval” state until the Organization Office of the 
Municipality of Turin performs a preliminary review of citizen reports, marking them as accepted 
or rejected. The possible states for a report are: Pending Approval, In Progress, Work in Progress, 
Suspended, Rejected. After approval, accepted reports move to the “In Progress” state, at which 
point they are assigned to the technical office responsible, based on the problem category. Once 
the intervention is planned, the state changes to “Work in Progress”, indicating that the issue 
resolution has started. In some cases, for organizational or technical reasons, the report can be 
set to “Suspended”, awaiting further evaluation or resources. When the problem is solved, the 
technical office updates the status and closes the report. In case of rejection, a written explanation 
from the Organization Office is mandatory (see next section).  
If the intervention must be carried out by maintenance personnel from an external company (for 
example, Enel X for Public Lighting, or company Y for specific reports based on their content), 
two cases are possible: - Case 1: The company has access to Participium. In this case, the technical office assigns the 
report to users from the corresponding company. External maintenance personnel can move the 
report from Assigned to In Progress. Staff from the technical office and external maintenance 
workers can exchange information and comments through the report, but these are not visible to 
the reporting citizen (nor to other citizens). Once the work is completed, the external maintainer 
can mark the report as resolved. 
Note: Automatic assignment of all reports in a certain category to the external company 
(bypassing the initial review by the public relations officer of the municipality) is possible only if 
previously configured by the municipal administrator. - Case 2: The company does NOT have access to Participium. In this case, the external company 
updates the technical office outside Participium, and once the problems are solved, a staff 
member from the technical office will manually move the report to the Resolved state. 


C. CITIZEN UPDATES 
To strengthen trust between citizens and institutions, the citizen can receive updates regarding 
their own reports through various channels. First, at every state change, the citizen receives a 
notification on the platform with the corresponding update. Furthermore, municipal operators 
updating reports can send the reporting citizen a message through the platform, to which it can 
reply. The system must allow this functionality to be accessible by external chatbots as well. Each 
time the citizen receives a notification on the platform, they also get an email (this option can be 
disabled in the user settings panel, where they can also upload a personal photo). 
Moreover, after the approval phase, accepted reports immediately become visible on the 
Participium portal: they appear both on an interactive map of Turin, geolocated based on the 
citizen’s selected point, and in a summary table that allows filtering and sorting reports by 
category, status, or date. In both views, the reporter’s name (“anonymous” if that option was 
chosen) and the report title are displayed. Clicking on the title opens a page with the description.  
Even non-registered users can view both the maps and the summary table. Once logged into 
Participium, citizens can follow other citizens’ open reports and receive notifications (following the 
same rules as for their own reports). 


D. STATISTICS 
The system allows viewing public and private statistics. Public statistics are visible in a dedicated 
section of the website and concern the number of reports per category, and trends over day, week, 
or month. They are also visible to non-registered users. In the private section, accessible only to 
administrators, it is possible to view, in addition to the public statistics, charts and tables.

branch_003.rationale: The original High-Level Goal 'Keep citizens informed about report progress' is well-supported by Section C of the documentation, which details notifications for state changes, messages from operators, and email alerts. The bottom-up reconstruction 'Keep Registered Citizens informed about their report status' is semantically equivalent but slightly less comprehensive, as 'progress' encompasses both status changes and the interactive communication (messages) described in the text. The original goal is distinct from 'Allow citizens to track other urban issues' (which focuses on following *other* citizens' reports) and 'Enable citizens to report urban inconveniences' (submission). Therefore, the original goal is accurate, appropriately scoped, and should be kept. The parent HLG 'Keep citizens informed about report progress' is supported by Section C of the documentation, which specifies that citizens receive notifications on state changes, can receive messages from operators, and can view the status of their reports. The current LLGs cover 'receiving real-time notifications on report status changes' (LLG_001) and 'viewing the detailed progress history' (LLG_002). While the documentation also mentions the ability to receive and reply to messages from municipal operators, this interactive communication feature is often considered part of the broader 'communication' or 'support' workflow rather than the core 'progress tracking' status update mechanism. However, looking closely at the documentation: 'municipal operators updating reports can send the reporting citizen a message through the platform, to which it can reply.' This is a distinct capability from passive status notifications. Is it essential to 'Keep citizens informed about report progress'? The HLG description says 'receive timely notifications and updates on the status changes and progress'. The message feature is a channel for updates. However, LLG_001 covers 'notifications on report status changes'. The message feature is a two-way communication. If we strictly interpret 'progress' as status updates, the current LLGs are sufficient. If we interpret 'informed' broadly to include operator messages, it might be missing. But typically, 'progress' refers to the lifecycle state. The sibling HLG 'Allow citizens to track other urban issues' covers following others. The current LLGs focus on the citizen's own reports. The documentation states: 'at every state change, the citizen receives a notification... Furthermore, municipal operators... can send... a message'. The message is an additional channel. Given the conservative instruction to regenerate only if an *essential* capability is absent, and that status notifications (LLG_001) and history viewing (LLG_002) cover the core 'progress' aspect, the message feature might be seen as an enhancement or part of a separate communication goal. However, the HLG description explicitly mentions 'updates'. The message is an update. But is it *essential* to the definition of 'progress'? Usually, progress is the state. The message is content. I will consider the current LLGs sufficient for the core 'progress' tracking, as the primary mechanism for progress awareness is the status change notification. The message feature is a specific interaction type. Without a specific HLG for 'Communicate with operators', it's ambiguous. But 'Keep informed' is primarily about status. I will keep the LLGs.

missing_hlg_evaluation.rationale:
The project description outlines the functional responsibilities for all identified actors, and the current High-Level Goals (HLGs) comprehensively cover these intentions. 

1. **Registered Citizen**: Goals cover reporting (submission, privacy/anonymity), tracking (own and others' reports), and communication (notifications/updates). The user settings (photo upload, email toggle) are minor configuration details typically subsumed under general account management or privacy, not distinct high-level functional goals.
2. **Non-Registered User**: Goals cover viewing public reports (map/table) and public statistics. This fully matches the description.
3. **Organization Office Staff**: Goals cover preliminary review (accept/reject) and communication of rejections. This matches the description.
4. **Technical Office Staff**: Goals cover workflow management (assignment, status updates, closing) and collaboration with external maintenance. This matches the description.
5. **External Maintenance Personnel**: Goals cover receiving assigned reports and communicating with technical staff. This matches the description.
6. **Municipal Administrator**: Goals cover system configuration (automatic assignment rules) and accessing comprehensive statistics (public and private). This matches the description.

No distinct functional actor-level intentions are missing from the current HLG list. All documented workflows and responsibilities are mapped to existing goals.

branch_001.rationale: The original High-Level Goal 'Enable citizens to report urban inconveniences' accurately captures the core functional intention of the Registered Citizen actor as described in the project documentation (Section A: REPORTS). The bottom-up reconstruction 'Enable Registered Citizens to submit comprehensive urban inconvenience reports' is semantically equivalent, merely adding the adjective 'comprehensive' to reflect the mandatory fields (location, description, category, photos). The original goal is not too generic, narrow, or ambiguous; it correctly identifies the actor's primary purpose in the system. There is no overlap with other HLGs for this actor (registration, tracking, updates are distinct). Therefore, the original goal should be kept. The parent HLG 'Enable citizens to report urban inconveniences' explicitly includes the requirement that the system asks the citizen whether they want the report to be anonymous. The documentation states: 'After entering all the information and the pictures, the system asks the citizen whether they want the report to be anonymous'. The current LLGs cover location, description, category, and photos, but they do not include the capability to select the anonymity option. This is an essential part of the report submission process described in the documentation and is not covered by any other HLG (it is not part of registration, tracking, or public visibility). Therefore, the decomposition is incomplete.

branch_002.rationale: The original High-Level Goal 'Enable citizens to register and authenticate securely' is fully supported by the project description (Section A: REPORTS), which states that citizens must register with specific details, confirm via email link, and log in to use the system. The bottom-up reconstruction 'Facilitate Citizen System Access' is semantically equivalent but slightly less precise regarding the security/verification aspect emphasized in the documentation (email confirmation, valid registration). The original goal is appropriately scoped, distinct from other HLGs (reporting, tracking, updates), and accurately reflects the actor's need to establish a verified identity to access functionalities. Therefore, it should be kept. The parent HLG 'Enable citizens to register and authenticate securely' requires citizens to establish a verified account and log in. The documentation (Section A) specifies that registration involves submitting details (username, first name, last name), receiving an email with a confirmation link, and confirming via that link to activate the account. It also states that citizens must log in to use the system. The current LLGs cover: 1) submitting registration details (llg_001), 2) verifying the account using a token/link (llg_002), and 3) logging in to obtain an authentication token (llg_003). These LLGs collectively and accurately decompose the essential capabilities required for secure registration and authentication as described in the documentation. There are no missing essential capabilities for this specific HLG, and no LLGs are unsupported or misleading.

replacement_request.generation_project_description:
In the Municipality of Turin, a system called Participium is being developed — an information 
system that enables citizen participation in the management of urban environments. It allows 
citizens to interact with the public administration by reporting inconveniences and malfunctions 
found in the city (e.g., potholes in the asphalt, sidewalks with architectural barriers, garbage in the 
streets, broken streetlights, etc.). An example of a similar information system is IRIS in Venice: 
https://iris.sad.ve.it/. The system, once developed, will be made available as open-source 
software to all Italian public administrations through the portal https://developers.italia.it/.

A. REPORTS 
Citizens can submit reports only if they have registered in the system with a username, first name, 
and last name. Once the registration is received, the user gets an email with a confirmation link. 
The registration becomes valid, and the user can use the system only after confirming through 
that link. Once registered, a citizen can submit reports by selecting a point on the map of Turin 
(which will be saved with latitude and longitude values) and filling in a problem form with the 
following mandatory fields: title, textual description, category (chosen from a predefined list). It is 
also mandatory to attach one or more photos (up to 3 per report, with each photo stored with its 
file path on the server). The possible problem categories are: 
• Waterworks – Drinking water 
• Architectural Barriers 
• Sewerage 
• Public Lighting 
• Waste 
• Road Signs and Traffic Lights 
• Roads and Urban Furniture 
• Public Green Areas and Playgrounds 
• Other 
After entering all the information and the pictures, the system asks the citizen whether they want 
the report to be anonymous (the name will not appear in the public list of all reports).  

B. REPORT LIFECYCLE 
Once submitted, the report is in the “Pending Approval” state until the Organization Office of the 
Municipality of Turin performs a preliminary review of citizen reports, marking them as accepted 
or rejected. The possible states for a report are: Pending Approval, In Progress, Work in Progress, 
Suspended, Rejected. After approval, accepted reports move to the “In Progress” state, at which 
point they are assigned to the technical office responsible, based on the problem category. Once 
the intervention is planned, the state changes to “Work in Progress”, indicating that the issue 
resolution has started. In some cases, for organizational or technical reasons, the report can be 
set to “Suspended”, awaiting further evaluation or resources. When the problem is solved, the 
technical office updates the status and closes the report. In case of rejection, a written explanation 
from the Organization Office is mandatory (see next section).  
If the intervention must be carried out by maintenance personnel from an external company (for 
example, Enel X for Public Lighting, or company Y for specific reports based on their content), 
two cases are possible: - Case 1: The company has access to Participium. In this case, the technical office assigns the 
report to users from the corresponding company. External maintenance personnel can move the 
report from Assigned to In Progress. Staff from the technical office and external maintenance 
workers can exchange information and comments through the report, but these are not visible to 
the reporting citizen (nor to other citizens). Once the work is completed, the external maintainer 
can mark the report as resolved. 
Note: Automatic assignment of all reports in a certain category to the external company 
(bypassing the initial review by the public relations officer of the municipality) is possible only if 
previously configured by the municipal administrator. - Case 2: The company does NOT have access to Participium. In this case, the external company 
updates the technical office outside Participium, and once the problems are solved, a staff 
member from the technical office will manually move the report to the Resolved state. 


C. CITIZEN UPDATES 
To strengthen trust between citizens and institutions, the citizen can receive updates regarding 
their own reports through various channels. First, at every state change, the citizen receives a 
notification on the platform with the corresponding update. Furthermore, municipal operators 
updating reports can send the reporting citizen a message through the platform, to which it can 
reply. The system must allow this functionality to be accessible by external chatbots as well. Each 
time the citizen receives a notification on the platform, they also get an email (this option can be 
disabled in the user settings panel, where they can also upload a personal photo). 
Moreover, after the approval phase, accepted reports immediately become visible on the 
Participium portal: they appear both on an interactive map of Turin, geolocated based on the 
citizen’s selected point, and in a summary table that allows filtering and sorting reports by 
category, status, or date. In both views, the reporter’s name (“anonymous” if that option was 
chosen) and the report title are displayed. Clicking on the title opens a page with the description.  
Even non-registered users can view both the maps and the summary table. Once logged into 
Participium, citizens can follow other citizens’ open reports and receive notifications (following the 
same rules as for their own reports). 


D. STATISTICS 
The system allows viewing public and private statistics. Public statistics are visible in a dedicated 
section of the website and concern the number of reports per category, and trends over day, week, 
or month. They are also visible to non-registered users. In the private section, accessible only to 
administrators, it is possible to view, in addition to the public statistics, charts and tables.

There are no missing essential capabilities for this specific HLG. The mention of 'first name' and 'last name' in the documentation is covered by the generic 'registration details' in llg_001, and the specific fields are implementation details rather than separate high-level capabilities. The LLGs are well-aligned with the parent goal and do not overlap with sibling HLGs.

branch_007.rationale:
The original High-Level Goal 'Enable Organization Office Staff to Conduct Preliminary Review of Submitted Reports' is explicitly supported by Section B of the project description, which states: 'Once submitted, the report is in the “Pending Approval” state until the Organization Office of the Municipality of Turin performs a preliminary review of citizen reports, marking them as accepted or rejected.' The goal accurately captures the actor's intention to manage the initial phase of the report lifecycle. While there is a sibling HLG 'Provide clear communication for rejected reports', that goal focuses specifically on the mandatory written explanation aspect, whereas the current goal covers the broader review process (access, evaluation, decision). Therefore, they are distinct functional intentions and should both be kept. The current Low-Level Goals (LLGs) accurately decompose the High-Level Goal (HLG) 'Enable Organization Office Staff to Conduct Preliminary Review of Submitted Reports'. 

1. **Retrieve Reports for Preliminary Review** (llg_001): Supports the need to access reports in the 'Pending Approval' state as described in Section B.
2. **Fetch Specific Report Details** (llg_002): Supports the evaluation phase where staff must examine the report content (title, description, category, photos) to make a decision.
3. **Accept Citizen Report** (llg_003): Supports the action of marking reports as accepted, which moves them to 'In Progress' as per Section B.
4. **Reject Citizen Report with Explanation** (llg_004): Supports the action of rejecting reports. The HLG description explicitly includes 'providing mandatory explanations for rejected reports'. While there is a sibling HLG 'Provide clear communication for rejected reports', the current HLG's description explicitly encompasses the provision of the explanation as part of the review decision process. Therefore, including the explanation in the rejection LLG is consistent with the parent HLG's scope and does not constitute a material defect or improper duplication that requires regeneration, especially since the sibling HLG likely focuses on the communication/notification aspect or the specific UI/UX of the explanation field, whereas this LLG focuses on the state transition and data persistence of the rejection decision. The decomposition covers all essential capabilities: access, evaluation, and decision-making (accept/reject with required data).
