replacement_request.generation_project_description:
In the Municipality of Turin, a system called Participium is being developed — an information 
system that enables citizen participation in the management of urban environments. It allows 
citizens to interact with the public administration by reporting inconveniences and malfunctions 
found in the city (e.g., potholes in the asphalt, sidewalks with architectural barriers, garbage in the 
streets, broken streetlights, etc.). An example of a similar information system is IRIS in Venice: 
https://iris.sad.ve.it/. The system, once developed, will be made available as open-source 
software to all Italian public administrations through the portal https://developers.italia.it/.

A. REPORTS 
Citizens can submit reports only if they have registered in the system with a username, first name, 
and last name. Once the registration is received, the user gets an email with a confirmation link. 
The registration becomes valid, and the user can use the system only after confirming through 
that link. Once registered, a citizen can submit reports by selecting a point on the map of Turin 
(which will be saved with latitude and longitude values) and filling in a problem form with the 
following mandatory fields: title, textual description, category (chosen from a predefined list). It is 
also mandatory to attach one or more photos (up to 3 per report, with each photo stored with its 
file path on the server). The possible problem categories are: 
• Waterworks – Drinking water 
• Architectural Barriers 
• Sewerage 
• Public Lighting 
• Waste 
• Road Signs and Traffic Lights 
• Roads and Urban Furniture 
• Public Green Areas and Playgrounds 
• Other 
After entering all the information and the pictures, the system asks the citizen whether they want 
the report to be anonymous (the name will not appear in the public list of all reports).  

B. REPORT LIFECYCLE 
Once submitted, the report is in the “Pending Approval” state until the Organization Office of the 
Municipality of Turin performs a preliminary review of citizen reports, marking them as accepted 
or rejected. The possible states for a report are: Pending Approval, In Progress, Work in Progress, 
Suspended, Rejected. After approval, accepted reports move to the “In Progress” state, at which 
point they are assigned to the technical office responsible, based on the problem category. Once 
the intervention is planned, the state changes to “Work in Progress”, indicating that the issue 
resolution has started. In some cases, for organizational or technical reasons, the report can be 
set to “Suspended”, awaiting further evaluation or resources. When the problem is solved, the 
technical office updates the status and closes the report. In case of rejection, a written explanation 
from the Organization Office is mandatory (see next section).  
If the intervention must be carried out by maintenance personnel from an external company (for 
example, Enel X for Public Lighting, or company Y for specific reports based on their content), 
two cases are possible: - Case 1: The company has access to Participium. In this case, the technical office assigns the 
report to users from the corresponding company. External maintenance personnel can move the 
report from Assigned to In Progress. Staff from the technical office and external maintenance 
workers can exchange information and comments through the report, but these are not visible to 
the reporting citizen (nor to other citizens). Once the work is completed, the external maintainer 
can mark the report as resolved. 
Note: Automatic assignment of all reports in a certain category to the external company 
(bypassing the initial review by the public relations officer of the municipality) is possible only if 
previously configured by the municipal administrator. - Case 2: The company does NOT have access to Participium. In this case, the external company 
updates the technical office outside Participium, and once the problems are solved, a staff 
member from the technical office will manually move the report to the Resolved state. 


C. CITIZEN UPDATES 
To strengthen trust between citizens and institutions, the citizen can receive updates regarding 
their own reports through various channels. First, at every state change, the citizen receives a 
notification on the platform with the corresponding update. Furthermore, municipal operators 
updating reports can send the reporting citizen a message through the platform, to which it can 
reply. The system must allow this functionality to be accessible by external chatbots as well. Each 
time the citizen receives a notification on the platform, they also get an email (this option can be 
disabled in the user settings panel, where they can also upload a personal photo). 
Moreover, after the approval phase, accepted reports immediately become visible on the 
Participium portal: they appear both on an interactive map of Turin, geolocated based on the 
citizen’s selected point, and in a summary table that allows filtering and sorting reports by 
category, status, or date. In both views, the reporter’s name (“anonymous” if that option was 
chosen) and the report title are displayed. Clicking on the title opens a page with the description.  
Even non-registered users can view both the maps and the summary table. Once logged into 
Participium, citizens can follow other citizens’ open reports and receive notifications (following the 
same rules as for their own reports). 


D. STATISTICS 
The system allows viewing public and private statistics. Public statistics are visible in a dedicated 
section of the website and concern the number of reports per category, and trends over day, week, 
or month. They are also visible to non-registered users. In the private section, accessible only to 
administrators, it is possible to view, in addition to the public statistics, charts and tables.

missing_hlg_evaluation.rationale:
The current High-Level Goals comprehensively cover all functional responsibilities described in the project documentation for each actor. 

1. **Registered Citizen**: Goals cover registration/authentication, report submission, tracking own reports (notifications/updates), and tracking other citizens' reports. The ability to manage personal settings (like disabling emails or uploading photos) is a minor configuration task typically subsumed under the broader goal of secure registration/authentication or general user management, and does not constitute a distinct high-level functional intention separate from the core participation workflow.
2. **Non-Registered User**: Goals cover viewing public reports (map/table) and accessing public statistics.
3. **Organization Office Staff**: Goals cover the preliminary review (accept/reject) and the specific requirement for providing explanations for rejections.
4. **Technical Office Staff**: Goals cover the core workflow management (assignment, status updates, closing) and collaboration with external maintenance.
5. **External Maintenance Personnel**: Goals cover managing assigned reports (status updates) and communication with the technical office.
6. **Municipal Administrator**: Goals cover configuring automatic routing and accessing comprehensive statistics/insights.

No distinct, unsupported, or missing functional intentions remain that are not already captured by the existing broad HLGs.

branch_001.rationale: The original High-Level Goal 'Enable citizens to report urban inconveniences' accurately captures the core functional intention of the Registered Citizen actor as described in Section A of the project documentation. The bottom-up reconstruction 'Enable Registered Citizens to submit comprehensive urban inconvenience reports' is semantically equivalent, merely adding the adjective 'comprehensive' to reflect the mandatory fields (location, description, category, photos). The original goal is supported, correctly scoped to the actor, and distinct from other goals like registration or tracking progress. There is no need to rewrite it as it is not too generic, narrow, or ambiguous. The parent HLG 'Enable citizens to report urban inconveniences' requires the submission of reports with specific mandatory fields: location, title, description, category, and photos, as well as the option for anonymity. The current LLGs cover the submission of location, description, and category (llg_001) and the upload of photos (llg_002). However, the documentation explicitly states that 'the system asks the citizen whether they want the report to be anonymous'. This is a distinct functional capability associated with the report submission process that is not covered by either of the current LLGs. While 'title' is also a mandatory field missing from llg_001's explicit description, the anonymity choice is a specific interaction step documented in Section A that is entirely absent from the decomposition. Therefore, the decomposition is incomplete.

The bottom-up reconstruction 'Facilitate Citizen System Access' is semantically equivalent but slightly less specific regarding the security/verification aspect emphasized in the original description ('securely', 'verified account'). The original goal is distinct from other Registered Citizen goals (reporting, tracking, following others) and correctly scoped to the onboarding and access control phase. Therefore, it should be kept. The parent HLG 'Enable citizens to register and authenticate securely' requires three main capabilities based on Section A: 1) Submitting registration details (username, first name, last name, email), 2) Verifying the account via a confirmation link, and 3) Logging in (authenticating) to use the system. The current LLGs cover these exactly: llg_001 covers submitting registration details, llg_002 covers verifying the account using the token/link, and llg_003 covers submitting credentials to log in and obtain an authentication token. All essential capabilities are present and correctly scoped to the Registered Citizen actor. There are no unsupported or misleading LLGs.

branch_003.rationale: The original High-Level Goal 'Keep citizens informed about report progress' is fully supported by Section C of the project description, which details that citizens receive notifications on the platform and via email at every state change of their own reports, and can also receive messages from municipal operators. The bottom-up reconstruction 'Keep Registered Citizens informed about their report status' is semantically equivalent but slightly less comprehensive as it omits the 'progress' aspect which includes operator messages and detailed updates, not just status changes. The original goal is distinct from 'Allow citizens to track other urban issues' (which covers following *other* citizens' reports) and 'Enable citizens to report urban inconveniences' (submission). Therefore, the original goal should be kept as it accurately captures the stakeholder intention for their own reports. The parent HLG 'Keep citizens informed about report progress' is supported by Section C, which states that citizens receive notifications on the platform and via email at every state change, and can also receive messages from municipal operators. The current LLGs cover receiving real-time notifications on status changes (llg_001) and viewing detailed progress history (llg_002). While the documentation mentions that municipal operators can send messages to the citizen, this is a specific communication channel that is arguably part of the broader 'updates' or 'progress' information. However, the core capability of being informed about status changes and progress is fully covered by the existing LLGs. The missing capability of receiving operator messages is a specific feature, but the primary goal of being informed about progress is met. Given the conservative instruction to regenerate only for essential missing capabilities or unsupported LLGs, and considering that 'progress' inherently includes status updates which are covered, the current decomposition is sufficient. The operator messaging feature is a specific implementation detail of how updates are delivered, but the core 'informed about progress' is satisfied by the status change notifications and history view. Therefore, no regeneration is needed.

The goal accurately captures the actor's intention to manage the initial phase of the report lifecycle. The bottom-up reconstruction 'Conduct Preliminary Review of Citizen Reports' is semantically equivalent but slightly less descriptive regarding the mandatory explanation aspect included in the original description. 4. 'Reject Citizen Report with Explanation' covers the rejection decision and explicitly includes the mandatory textual explanation required by Section B of the documentation ('In case of rejection, a written explanation from the Organization Office is mandatory').

branch_001.rationale: The original High-Level Goal 'Enable citizens to report urban inconveniences' is fully supported by the project description (Section A), which details the submission of reports with location, description, category, and photos. The bottom-up reconstruction 'Enable Registered Citizens to Submit Comprehensive Urban Inconvenience Reports' is semantically equivalent but slightly more verbose. The original goal is concise, accurately scoped to the actor's intention, and does not overlap with other HLGs (registration, tracking, updates). Therefore, it should be kept. The current Low-Level Goals (LLGs) fully cover the essential capabilities required by the parent High-Level Goal (HLG) 'Enable citizens to report urban inconveniences'. LLG_001 covers the submission of the report with title, location, description, category, and anonymity preference. LLG_002 covers the mandatory attachment of photos. The documentation (Section A) specifies that citizens must select a point on the map (location), fill in mandatory fields (title, description, category), attach photos, and choose anonymity. Both LLGs align with these requirements. There are no missing essential capabilities, and no LLGs are unsupported or misleading. The decomposition is complete and accurate.

branch_008.rationale: The original High-Level Goal 'Efficiently manage report resolution workflow' is fully supported by the project description (Section B), which details the Technical Office Staff's role in assigning reports, planning interventions, updating statuses (In Progress, Work in Progress, Suspended, Resolved), and closing reports. The bottom-up reconstruction 'Enable Technical Office Staff to Manage and Track Report Resolution' is semantically equivalent but slightly less precise regarding the 'workflow' aspect (which includes state transitions and assignment). The original goal is concise, accurately scoped to the actor's core operational responsibility, and distinct from the other Technical Office Staff HLG 'Facilitate collaboration with external maintenance' (which focuses specifically on communication). Therefore, the original goal should be kept. The current Low-Level Goals (LLGs) cover the core workflow steps for the Technical Office Staff: retrieving approved reports (llg_001), assigning them (llg_002), updating status to 'In Progress' (llg_003), and updating status to 'Resolved' (llg_004). The parent HLG 'Efficiently manage report resolution workflow' is fully supported by these LLGs. The documentation (Section B) states that the technical office assigns reports, plans interventions (implied by moving to 'Work in Progress' or 'In Progress'), and updates statuses. While the documentation mentions a 'Work in Progress' state, the LLG 'Enable Technical Office Staff to update a report's status to In Progress' (llg_003) and 'Resolved' (llg_004) cover the primary state transitions managed by the Technical Office. The 'Work in Progress' state is often a sub-state or a specific transition that might be handled within the same update mechanism or is considered part of the general status management. More importantly, the core capabilities of assignment and resolution tracking are present. There are no unsupported LLGs. The missing 'Work in Progress' specific update is a minor granularity issue, but the general capability to manage the lifecycle is present. However, looking closely at Section B: 'Once the intervention is planned, the state changes to “Work in Progress”'. The Technical Office is responsible for this. Is it essential to have a specific LLG for 'Work in Progress'? The parent HLG says 'manage their lifecycle from In Progress to Resolved'. The LLGs cover In Progress and Resolved. The 'Work in Progress' state is an intermediate step. Given the conservative instruction to not regenerate for optional lifecycle operations or granularity, and that the core workflow (assign -> start -> resolve) is covered, the decomposition is sufficient. The 'Work in Progress' state is a specific status update, but the general ability to update status is implied or covered by the specific status updates listed. If we consider 'Work in Progress' essential, it is missing. However, 'In Progress' is the state after assignment. 'Work in Progress' is when work starts. The LLG llg_003 says 'update... to In Progress when work begins'. This conflates the two states or treats 'In Progress' as the start of work. The documentation distinguishes 'In Progress' (assigned) and 'Work in Progress' (intervention started). The LLG llg_003 description says 'change the status... to In Progress when work begins'. This is slightly inaccurate regarding the state name vs timing, but functionally it covers the transition to the active work phase. The missing explicit 'Work in Progress' update is a minor gap. However, the prompt asks to decide conservatively. The core capabilities are present. I will keep the LLGs.

missing_hlg_evaluation.rationale:
The current High-Level Goals comprehensively cover all functional responsibilities described in the project documentation for each actor. 

1. **Registered Citizen**: Goals cover registration/authentication, reporting (with all mandatory fields and anonymity), tracking own reports (notifications/updates), and tracking other citizens' reports (following). The description mentions 'user settings panel' for disabling emails and uploading photos, but this is a minor configuration detail typically subsumed under account management or the reporting/notification goals, not a distinct high-level functional intention requiring a separate HLG.
2. **Non-Registered User**: Goals cover viewing public reports (map/table) and public statistics. This aligns with Section C and D.
3. **Organization Office Staff**: Goal covers preliminary review (accept/reject) and mandatory explanations. This aligns with Section B.
4. **Technical Office Staff**: Goals cover managing the resolution workflow (assignment, status updates, closing) and facilitating collaboration with external maintenance. This aligns with Section B, including both cases where external companies have access and where they do not (manual update by technical staff).
5. **External Maintenance Personnel**: Goals cover managing assigned reports (status updates) and communication with technical staff. This aligns with Section B, Case 1.
6. **Municipal Administrator**: Goals cover configuring automatic routing and accessing comprehensive statistics (public and private). This aligns with Section B (note on automatic assignment) and Section D.

No distinct, unsupported, or missing functional intentions were identified that are not already covered by the existing broad HLGs.
